2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: High concern — Between 2011 and 2023, the national universe of rural public elementary schools contracted from 56,544 to 34,406 (a net reduction of 22,138 schools, or 39.2%; PDF p. 3). Restricting the analytic dataset exclusively to schools that remained active and linked to the same municipality in both 2011 and 2023 excludes closed or paralyzed schools without comparing their baseline WASH deprivation against surviving schools.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern — Multivariable binomial logistic regressions adjust for macroregion, differentiated territorial status, enrollment size, municipal population brackets, rural population percentage and municipal IDHM-income (PDF pp. 5, 8-10), but omit school administrative dependency (state vs. municipal networks) and municipal water/sewerage utility coverage, fail to account for municipal-level clustering, and include endogenous/mutually dependent student yield variables (approval, failure and dropout rates) on the right-hand side as determinants of WASH absence, introducing reverse-causality and collider bias.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate concern (adequate administrative coding of territorial designations; no direct program exposure measurement) — Legal-territorial school categories ('Localização diferenciada': settlement areas, Indigenous lands, quilombola communities, and traditional peoples/communities added in 2023) and rural public elementary school status under Lei nº 9.394/1996 (excluding EJA) are coded directly from official Inep School Census registries (Quadro 1, PDF p. 5). However, federal institutional funding and WASH programs (Funasa Programa Água na Escola, PDDE per-capita funding rules, and PAR) are invoked only narratively in the Introduction and Discussion rather than measured at the school or municipal level (PDF pp. 2, 10-11).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern — School-level WASH and infrastructure data in the Inep Censo Escolar are self-declared by school principals without systematic external verification ('autodeclarados pelos diretores escolares e não passem por auditoria sistemática', PDF p. 3), with Inep acknowledging major questionnaire errors in other waves (2007-2010, 2017). Additionally, municipal IDHM-income from 2010 was reused for the 2023 cross-section because updated post-2022 IDHM data were unavailable (PDF p. 3), and category 8 ('povos e comunidades tradicionais') existed only in 2023 (PDF p. 5).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: High concern — School WASH outcomes are restricted to three crude, unverified self-reported binary indicators in the Censo Escolar: complete absence of water supply, complete absence of sanitation/sewerage, and existence of any toilet (Quadro 1, PDF pp. 5-6). These proxies do not capture drinking-water potability or safety, supply continuity, toilet functionality/privacy, handwashing stations with soap, or menstrual hygiene facilities.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern — No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported, and full multivariable logistic regression tables are omitted from the article. The Results section selectively reports prose odds ratios and p-values for highlighted categories (PDF pp. 9-10) without 95% confidence intervals, standard errors, exact regression sample sizes, or model fit/collinearity diagnostics.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern — Although drawn from the nationwide Inep School Census covering 3,424 municipalities, inclusion was conditioned on survival: only rural public elementary schools that remained active and linked to the same municipality in both 2011 and 2023 were retained (PDF p. 3). Because 22,138 rural schools closed or ceased offering regular elementary education over this period, survivor selection bias likely understates historical WASH deprivation among the smallest and most vulnerable closed schools.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion and exclusion rules are clearly stated: Brazilian rural public elementary schools (Ensino Fundamental, excluding EJA / adult education) recorded in the Inep Censo Escolar da Educação Básica that remained active and linked to the same municipality in both 2011 and 2023, with explicit rationale for excluding 2007-2010 and 2017 (questionnaire inconsistencies) and 2020-2021 (COVID-19 suspension of in-person classes). While the inclusion rule itself is unambiguous, conditioning inclusion on 12-year school survival introduces survivor selection bias (captured under cross-tool selection_bias and attrition).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The institutional and geographic setting—Brazilian rural public elementary schools across 3,424 municipalities and all five macroregions in 2011 and 2023—is described in detail across school-level characteristics (differentiated territorial location including Indigenous lands, settlements, quilombos and traditional communities; enrollment brackets; approval, failure and dropout rates) and municipal-level characteristics (population size, rural population share and IDHM-income), although Tables 1 and 2 report subgroup percentages without printing cell sample-size denominators in text.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Explanatory territorial, demographic and socioeconomic variables are drawn from official national statistical registries: Inep Censo Escolar (school territorial category, enrollment size, student yield rates), IBGE Censo Demográfico 2010 and 2022 (macroregion, municipal population, rural population percentage) and PNUD/IPEA AtlasBR (municipal IDHM-income). Caveats transparently noted by the authors include reliance on lagged 2010 IDHM-income for the 2023 model due to data availability, addition of traditional-communities coding only in 2023, and lack of systematic external audit for principal-reported school attributes.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 3, 5, Métodos — Banco de dados; Variáveis analisadas; Quadro 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Although standardized national Inep Censo Escolar questionnaire items and binary coding definitions were applied uniformly across schools (Quadro 1), the presence or absence of school water supply, sanitation and toilets is self-declared by school principals without systematic external verification or physical inspection ('autodeclarados pelos diretores escolares e não passem por auditoria sistemática'), failing the requirement for objective measurement criteria.

domain_ratings.justification: The study identifies key geographic, territorial, demographic, socioeconomic and school-scale factors associated with rural school WASH infrastructure—macroregion, differentiated territorial status, school enrollment size, municipal population size, rural population share and municipal IDHM-income (Quadro 1)—though it omits school administrative dependency (state vs. municipal network) and municipal household water/sanitation coverage.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5-6, 8-10, Métodos — Variáveis analisadas (Quadro 1); Resultados — Fatores determinantes da ausência de WASH

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors state and implement multivariable binomial logistic regression for 2011 and 2023 to adjust simultaneously for school-level and municipal-level covariates that passed bivariate chi-square screening at the 5% level. However, including endogenous educational performance outcomes (approval, failure and dropout rates) as explanatory covariates introduces potential reverse-causality and collider bias.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6, 8, Métodos — Tratamento estatístico; Resultados — Fatores determinantes da ausência de WASH

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors selected 2011 and 2023 after technical dialogue with Inep to avoid severe historical questionnaire anomalies documented in 2007-2010 and 2017. Nevertheless, reliability and construct validity remain uncertain because Censo Escolar WASH responses are unverified principal self-declarations and measure only crude binary absence of any water source, any sewerage/sanitation system or any toilet—providing no information on water potability, service continuity, functional toilets, soap/handwashing stations or menstrual hygiene adequacy.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 3, 5-6, Métodos — Banco de dados; Variáveis analisadas; Quadro 1

domain_ratings.justification: Several analytical flaws undermine the regression models: (1) school-level and municipal-level variables across 3,424 municipalities are entered into single-level binomial logistic regressions without multilevel modeling or municipality-clustered standard errors; (2) mutually dependent and endogenous student yield rates (approval, failure and dropout rates) are entered simultaneously as 'determinants' of WASH infrastructure despite reverse causality and collinearity; (3) covariates are selected via bivariate chi-square p < 0.05 screening; (4) paired temporal correlation within the same surviving schools between 2011 and 2023 is not modeled; and (5) full regression tables, 95% confidence intervals, standard errors and model diagnostics are omitted from the text.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: High concern (JBI narrative judgment; no numeric score). Corrêa et al. (2026) conduct a nationwide comparative analytical cross-sectional study of WASH absence in Brazilian rural public elementary schools in 2011 and 2023 using Inep School Census and IBGE municipal census data across 3,424 municipalities. Strengths include comprehensive national territorial coverage, transparent variable definitions (Quadro 1), and proactive technical consultation with Inep to avoid known historical questionnaire-error waves (2007-2010 and 2017). Large descriptive disparities—particularly acute WASH deprivation in the North region, on Indigenous lands, and in micro-schools with up to 10 students—are clearly documented in Tables 1 and 2. However, substantial methodological risks affect internal validity, especially for the multivariable regression claims: (1) restricting the sample to schools active in the same municipality in both 2011 and 2023 amid a 39.2% contraction of rural public elementary schools (22,138 closures) introduces severe survivor bias; (2) WASH outcomes rely on unverified principal self-declarations of crude binary absence/presence without potability, functionality, handwashing or menstrual-hygiene measures; (3) single-level binomial logistic regressions combine school- and municipal-level covariates without accounting for clustering within 3,424 municipalities and include endogenous, collinear student flow outcomes (approval, failure and dropout rates) as 'determinants' of WASH absence; and (4) full regression tables and 95% confidence intervals are omitted in favor of selective prose odds ratios and p-values.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Repeated/comparative analytical cross-sectional study using national administrative school census and demographic census microdata (descriptive spatial/tabular analysis and separate binomial logistic regressions for 2011 and 2023)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design and objectives: PDF p. 1 (Resumo), pp. 2-3 (Introdução), p. 14 (Abstract). Population, school closure counts, data sources, self-reporting limitations, year selection rationale, and survivor inclusion rule: PDF pp. 3-4 (Métodos — Área de estudo; Banco de dados; Figura 1). Variable definitions and WASH binary coding: PDF pp. 5-6 (Métodos — Variáveis analisadas; Quadro 1). Statistical methods: PDF p. 6 (Métodos — Tratamento estatístico) and p. 8 (Resultados — Fatores determinantes). Descriptive and regression findings: PDF pp. 6-10 (Resultados, Figura 2, Tabela 1, Tabela 2). Institutional context (PDDE funding formula, Funasa, PAR) and substantive interpretation: PDF pp. 2, 10-11 (Introdução; Discussão; Conclusão).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study explicitly adopts a comparative cross-sectional observational design ('um estudo transversal e comparativo referente aos anos de 2011 e 2023') using descriptive cross-tabulations and separate binomial logistic regressions in 2011 and 2023 to estimate school-level and municipal-level determinants of WASH absence. No specific policy or legal intervention is evaluated with a treatment/comparator counterfactual (ruling out ROBINS-I), and schools are not followed as baseline outcome-free cohorts to estimate incidence over time (ruling out JBI Cohort). Accordingly, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
